title: Trump Was Always an Iran Hawk
author: Matthew Schmitz
content:
![Trump Was Always an Iran
Hawk](https://www.compactmag.com/content/images/2026/03/Screenshot-2026-03-01-at-10.27.13
---PM-1.png)

For more than four decades, Donald Trump has called for invading Iran, seizing
its oil, and preventing it from gaining a nuclear weapon. You wouldn't know
this if you listened to some of Trump's erstwhile supporters. In the wake of
his latest attack on Iran, they accuse him of betraying the America First
movement. "This isn't stabbing Trump's original followers in the back. It's
stabbing them in the front," [_says_](https://spectator.com/article/is-this-
trumps-sarajevo-moment-iran/?edition=us&ref=compactmag.com) _American
Conservative_ editor Curt Mills.

Trump has always taken a less idealistic approach to foreign policy than do
neoconservative interventionists or liberal internationalists. He has
frequently and opportunistically attacked his opponents as warmongers. But his
problem with "forever wars" was not that they involved bloodshed; it was that
they didn't end in victory.

Trump's Iran-hawk bona fides go back to 1980, when he gave what the historians
Charlie Laderman and Brendan Simms
[_describe_](https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/donald-
trump-9781788310482/?ref=compactmag.com) as his "earliest recorded statement
on foreign policy to a national audience."

In an interview with NBC, Trump complained that the Iran hostage crisis was a
sign that America no longer commanded international respect. His interviewer
replied, "Obviously you're advocating that we should have gone in there with
troops, et cetera, and brought our boys out like Vietnam." Trump replied: "I
absolutely feel that, yes."

Trump then worried aloud that the Iran-Iraq war could develop into a larger
conflict because the United States "is not more involved in terms of setting
policy in that area." This interview set the pattern for the coming decades.

In a 1987 speech in New Hampshire, Trump
[_suggested_](https://www.nytimes.com/1987/10/23/nyregion/new-hampshire-
speech-earns-praise-for-trump.html?ref=compactmag.com), in the words of _The
New York Times_ , that the United States should "attack Iran and seize some of
its oil fields in retaliation for … Iran's bullying of America."

In 1988, Trump
[_told_](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2017/jan/12/polly-
toynbee-1988-interview-donald-trump?ref=compactmag.com) _The Guardian_ , "I'd
be harsh on Iran. They've been beating us psychologically, making us look a
bunch of fools. One bullet shot at one of our men or ships and I'd do a number
on Kharg Island," an Iranian oil hub.

In 2000, Trump [_complained_](https://www.ebroadsheet.com/wp-
content/uploads/2017/03/playboy-interview-donald-
trump-1990?ref=compactmag.com) again about how Jimmy Carter had handled Iran
and said that as president he would "believe very strongly in extreme military
strength."

In 2007, Trump
[_said_](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2007/jan/07/media.citynews?ref=compactmag.com),
after being asked what he'd do if he were president, "First, I'd try and solve
the problems in the Middle East."

In 2011, Trump [_told_](https://www.foxnews.com/transcript/donald-trump-on-
the-oreilly-factor-part-2?ref=compactmag.com) Bill O'Reilly, "I wouldn't let
them have a nuke"--referring to Iran. He then dismissed Barack Obama as a
"weak president that kisses everybody's ass."

In 2020, after killing General Qasem Soleimani, Trump
[_warned_](https://x.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1213593975732527112?ref=compactmag.com)
that any retaliation from Iran would result in his hitting Iranian cultural
sites "very fast and very hard."

In 2024, after intelligence officials told Trump that Iran was attempting to
assassinate him, Trump
[_declared_](https://x.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1838802596066209994?ref=compactmag.com),
"An attack on a former President is a Death Wish for the attacker!"

Given this record, it isn't exactly surprising that Trump ordered strikes on
Iran's nuclear sites in 2025, or that he has now launched a more ambitious
attack on Iran.

It is true that Trump often
[_presented_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/28/us/politics/trump-peace-
president-war.html?ref=compactmag.com) himself as the anti-war candidate. But
just as frequently, he indicated his readiness to use military force. He was
more restrained in his first term than he has been in his second, making it
easier to [_see him_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/trump-s-real-crime-
is-opposing-empire/) as a non-interventionist. And he brought into his second
administration several people identified with foreign-policy restraint. But
his overall record indicated a readiness to vindicate American honor and
advance American interests, rather than a rejection of foreign conflicts. Even
as Trump
[_claimed_](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/114931438809653171?ref=compactmag.com)
to be the "president of peace," he
[_spoke_](https://news.un.org/en/story/2020/09/1073002?ref=compactmag.com) of
achieving "peace through strength."

It is understandable that non-interventionists are disappointed in Trump. But
many have gone further, accusing him of a radical about-face brought about by
undue influence from Israel. Both [_Dean
Baker_](https://x.com/DeanBaker13/status/2027901907470324137?ref=compactmag.com),
the establishment liberal economist, and [_Candace
Owens_](https://x.com/RealCandaceO/status/2027807142686683203?ref=compactmag.com),
the anti-establishment right-wing podcaster, have begun referring to
"Operation Epstein Fury." Curt Mills
[_says_](https://x.com/CurtMills/status/2028168125242360207?ref=compactmag.com)
that Trump has been "conned and bullied by Israeli hawks and Capitol Hill
neocons."

> "Trump's actions should be blamed on--or credited to--himself."

But there was no need to con or bully Trump into a course of action he was
always ready to pursue. Trump's actions should be blamed on--or credited to--
himself and his supporters, rather than any foreign country. Here as
elsewhere, talk of Israeli conspiracy has become a way for MAGA influencers to
explain away the gap between their claims about Trump during the campaign, and
his record since entering office.

Precisely because this war reflects Trump's priorities, it will be an
important test for his vision of foreign policy. There are reasons to
[_doubt_](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/02/27/trump-war-
iran/?ref=compactmag.com) the prudence of Trump's latest move. But as Stephen
Wertheim has
[_noted_](https://x.com/stephenwertheim/status/2027780095625073004?ref=compactmag.com),
the fact that Trump does not care about democracy promotion gives him greater
freedom of movement than George W. Bush enjoyed. Just as Trump's actual
foreign policy views never constrained him from launching this attack, they
may leave him freer to bring it to an end.
